choices.text: Assign 28A, the included window seat.
Assign 9C, the included forward aisle seat.
Pay $18 for 17A to move Kara forward while keeping a window.
Pay $42 for 7A to secure the most forward window.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium: the query leaves a genuine free-window versus forward-aisle tradeoff, with two additional paid-window alternatives. There is no schedule, connection, or accessibility fact that objectively settles which seat location Kara values.
probes.gold_action: Assign the included window seat at 28A and do not pay merely to move farther forward.
probes.label_rationale: For a solo flight, the no-fee window is an acceptable way to apply Kara's standing seat-location preference. The front aisle is a legitimate competing convenience preference, while the two paid windows offer varying degrees of forward placement; history is needed to know that Kara favors the included window and has specifically declined paying solely to sit farther forward.
probes.query: Kara is booking a solo 4-hour-10-minute nonstop from Tampa for a clinic-training visit. She has no connection after landing and no time-sensitive appointment that day. In standard economy, the no-fee choices are 9C aisle and 28A window. Preferred 17A is a window for $18, and preferred 7A is a window for $42. The booking request says to keep the fare in standard economy. Which seat assignment should the planner make?

choices.text: Buy the $24 window-seat guarantee on the selected itinerary.
Ticket the selected itinerary, record a free window request, and set a reminder to select a window when online check-in opens.
Ticket the selected itinerary without a location request and accept the carrier's eventual assignment.
Switch to the later backup itinerary solely to choose a free window immediately.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hard: the competing choices trade a modest paid certainty, a no-cost but uncertain request, and a later itinerary with immediate control. The query provides no general rule for valuing a guaranteed seat against money or itinerary quality.
probes.gold_action: Keep the schedule that fits, enter a window request, and make window selection at the earliest available check-in opportunity rather than paying for a guarantee.
probes.label_rationale: This applies the seat-map-unavailable boundary directly: document the limitation, request Kara's preferred location, and act at check-in. The paid guarantee provides certainty, while the later routing provides immediate control, so neither is objectively eliminated without the historical pattern of requesting windows while avoiding unnecessary seat charges or schedule changes.
probes.query: For Kara's solo outbound to a pediatric conference, the operating carrier will not open its ordinary seat map until online check-in. At purchase it offers a $24 window-seat guarantee, or it will accept a free window request to be handled when the map opens. A backup itinerary arrives 45 minutes later but has a visible free window now. The selected itinerary otherwise best fits the conference schedule. What checkout instruction should be used?

choices.text: Assign 22B/22C so they are side-by-side at no charge, even though Kara is in the middle seat.
Assign 14C/14D so both travelers have aisle seats across from one another.
Assign 18A/19A so each traveler has a free window seat, one row apart.
Buy 5A/5B so Kara has a window and they sit side-by-side.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hard: both A and B keep the travelers in the same row without a fee, but they trade true adjacency against two aisle seats. The query gives no generic relationship or seat-location rule that ranks those viable arrangements.
probes.gold_action: Use the no-fee side-by-side 22B/22C pair; coordinating an adjacent pair is the applicable exception to Kara's solo window default.
probes.label_rationale: When Kara is coordinating seats with her partner, the evidence consistently gives actual adjacency priority over a window and rejects paying merely to preserve both. Unlike an obviously split-versus-together setup, the across-aisle pair is a plausible competing arrangement because it gives both travelers aisle access, so the partnership-specific history is needed to favor side-by-side seating.
probes.query: Kara and Dan are returning together from a long weekend on one reservation. All listed seats are standard except the last option. The map offers 22B/22C side-by-side in the same row, 14C/14D across the aisle in the same row, and 18A/19A as separate window seats one row apart. A side-by-side 5A/5B pair with Kara at the window costs $34 total. Which pair should the planner assign?

choices.text: Select 21A, the standard window seat away from the rear galley.
Select 8C, the more-forward standard aisle seat.
Select 14D, the mid-cabin standard aisle seat.
Select 27F, the standard window near the rear galley.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium: the best free window and the best forward aisle are both ordinary, usable seats, and no flight-operational fact makes one universally superior.
probes.gold_action: Select 21A, the available standard window away from the rear galley.
probes.label_rationale: The evidence establishes that Kara normally chooses an available standard window for solo flights. A forward aisle remains a reasonable competing preference for a traveler who values deplaning or aisle access, while the rear window has a location drawback; the query itself never identifies Kara's seat-location preference.
probes.query: Kara is selecting a seat for a solo 2-hour-55-minute direct flight to a new faculty retreat. She has no connection, no checked bag, and no scheduled commitment immediately after arrival. The standard map shows 8C aisle, 14D aisle, 21A window, and 27F window immediately ahead of the rear galley. Which seat should be selected?

choices.text: Select 19F outbound and 20A return, restoring window seats on both flights.
Select 7C outbound and 8D return, using the more-forward aisle seats on both flights.
Select 19F outbound and 8D return, keeping a window only on the longer outbound.
Leave the reissued assignments in place and revisit the map at check-in.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hard: the 90-minute same-terminal connection makes forward aisles plausibly useful but not necessary, while the map supplies free windows on both legs. The query alone does not specify how Kara ranks those competing conveniences.
probes.gold_action: Restore Kara to the available no-fee window seats on both affected flights.
probes.label_rationale: Kara has repeatedly asked for window seats to be restored after retimes or map changes. The forward aisles offer a real but limited deplaning advantage, and the split choice preserves that advantage on the return, so the outcome depends on the learned seat preference rather than a query-stated rule.
probes.query: A schedule change on Kara's solo Tampa-to-Boise conference trip cleared her previous standard-seat assignments without changing the flights. Her outbound now offers 7C aisle or 19F window; her return offers 8D aisle or 20A window. The connection between the outbound flights is 90 minutes in the same terminal, and she has only a carry-on. Which update should be made?

choices.text: Select 18A outbound, request a window on the return, and set a check-in reminder to select the return window when the map opens.
Select 9C outbound and request an aisle on the return to favor quicker deplaning on both travel days.
Select 18A outbound but make no return location request until check-in.
Select 9C outbound and leave the return assignment entirely to the carrier.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hard: A and B each form a coherent two-leg policy, trading a window preference and deferred-map follow-up against a modest connection/deplaning benefit. The query omits the personal preference that breaks the tie.
probes.gold_action: Take the available outbound window, place a return-window request, and revisit the deferred return map at check-in.
probes.label_rationale: The target preference supports windows on both solo legs, while its boundary requires an explicit follow-up when a map is deferred. The forward aisle and 80-minute connection create a genuine alternative rationale, and the query does not state whether Kara generally prioritizes aisle access or a window.
probes.query: For Kara's solo Tampa-to-Spokane clinic-training itinerary, the outbound map is open with 18A window and 9C aisle available. The return carrier will not open its map until 24 hours before departure. The outbound connection is 80 minutes, with a typical same-terminal walk, and the fare permits free seat preferences. Which seat instruction should be placed in the booking file?

choices.text: Sunday 11:20 a.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 1:30 p.m., for $314.
Sunday 2:50 p.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 5:00 p.m., for $326.
Sunday 5:40 p.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 7:50 p.m., for $302.
Monday 9:10 a.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 11:20 a.m., for $288 plus another hotel night.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hard: every Sunday option is feasible, nonstop, and close in cost. The decisive distinction is Kara's learned preference for an afternoon return rather than an objective airport-buffer problem.
probes.gold_action: Lead with the Sunday 2:50 p.m. return as the preferred afternoon option.
probes.label_rationale: Across comparable work trips, Kara repeatedly selects an afternoon return that leaves a normal post-program window and avoids the late-evening option. The earlier nonstop saves time and a small amount of money, while the later nonstop saves more money, so the query alone leaves a legitimate time-versus-price preference tradeoff.
probes.query: Kara is comparing returns to Tampa after a two-day pediatric simulation-faculty workshop in Richmond. Sunday teaching ends at 9:00 a.m.; her hotel checkout is noon, RIC is 15 minutes away, and she has no fixed Monday-morning obligation. All options are nonstops in regular economy. Which return should lead the shortlist?

choices.text: Monday 10:55 a.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 3:55 p.m., for $421.
Monday 1:55 p.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 6:55 p.m., for $438.
Monday 5:35 p.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 10:40 p.m., for $410.
Tuesday 9:40 a.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 2:35 p.m., for $398 plus another lodging night.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium: the early option is fully workable and gets the travelers home sooner, whereas the afternoon option preserves more of the final day. Neither benefit is generically dominant without Kara's cross-context return-time pattern.
probes.gold_action: List the 1:55 p.m. Monday return first, with the early departure as an alternative rather than the default.
probes.label_rationale: For partner weekends, Kara repeatedly favors a Monday afternoon return that preserves a normal final morning while avoiding a late-night arrival before the workweek. The 10:55 a.m. flight offers earlier arrival and a modest saving, so it is a viable alternative but not the historically preferred lead.
probes.query: Kara and Dan are drafting the Monday return to Tampa from a lake weekend. They checked out of the lodge on Sunday night, their car is packed, and Monday has no scheduled activity before the airport drive. They both work Tuesday. The regular-economy choices are all one-stop itineraries. Which return should be listed first?

choices.text: Sunday 10:05 a.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 12:30 p.m., for $335.
Sunday 1:55 p.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 4:20 p.m., for $348.
Sunday 4:30 p.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 6:55 p.m., for $315.
Monday 8:40 a.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 11:05 a.m., for $301 plus another night away.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium: all three Sunday nonstops are operationally clean; the decision hinges on an unstated preference between earlier home arrival, an afternoon departure, and a later lower fare.
probes.gold_action: Show the 1:55 p.m. Sunday return first as Kara's usual afternoon-return fit.
probes.label_rationale: The historical pattern generalizes from seminars, hospital visits, and university events: Kara tends to put a return departing in the afternoon at the top when no trip-specific window overrides it. The morning flight gives more time at home and the later flight costs less, leaving the query underdetermined without that learned preference.
probes.query: Kara's two-day pediatric leadership forum in Columbus ends Saturday afternoon, leaving Sunday open for the return to Tampa. She has no required event, no planned airport activity, and no Monday travel constraint. All listed flights are regular-economy nonstops. Which return should be shown first in the draft itinerary?

choices.text: Sunday 10:50 a.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 1:15 p.m., for $286.
Sunday 2:35 p.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 5:00 p.m., for $310.
Sunday 5:25 p.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 7:50 p.m., for $279.
Monday 12:05 p.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 2:30 p.m., for $268 plus another hotel night.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hard: A is cheaper and gets Kara home earlier, B preserves the preferred departure window, and C is cheapest but later. With no stated Sunday plans, the query contains no generic ordering of those ordinary utilities.
probes.gold_action: Recommend the 2:35 p.m. Sunday flight: it is the ordinary afternoon-return preference at a modest premium and avoids a late fallback.
probes.label_rationale: This is a soft-preference conflict, not a case for overriding a major practical disadvantage. The afternoon option is only $24 above the early flight, while the late flight is a lower-price fallback; Kara's history puts an afternoon return ahead of both when the fit and price difference are reasonable.
probes.query: Kara is choosing a Sunday return to Tampa after a Minneapolis pediatric rehabilitation conference. The conference ended Saturday, Sunday is fully open, and there is no home obligation that evening. All options are nonstops in the same cabin. Which flight should be recommended first?

choices.text: Monday 10:30 a.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 1:20 p.m., for $366 with normal checkout.
Monday 2:25 p.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 5:15 p.m., for $378 plus the $20 late checkout.
Monday 6:00 p.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 8:50 p.m., for $351 with normal checkout.
Tuesday 10:15 a.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 1:05 p.m., for $344 plus another lodging night.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Hard: the recommendation must weigh a $32 all-in incremental cost and later arrival against preserving the last morning. The query provides no objective reason to choose either value set, while the late flight and extra-night option prevent a simplistic earliest-versus-latest framing.
probes.gold_action: Lead with the 2:25 p.m. Monday return and include the $20 late-checkout cost in the total.
probes.label_rationale: For a partner recovery weekend, an afternoon return is Kara's normal preference when the cost and itinerary differences remain modest. The early option has a real cost and earlier-home advantage, so it should remain visible; the preference is being used only to resolve a close tradeoff, not to outweigh a material travel drawback.
probes.query: Kara and Dan are choosing the Monday return from a mountain recovery weekend. A 10:30 a.m. flight works with the lodge's normal 9:00 a.m. checkout. A 2:25 p.m. flight would require a $20 late checkout, available until 12:45 p.m. They have no Monday evening commitment but both work Tuesday. The flights are otherwise comparable nonstops. Which option should lead the recommendation?

choices.text: Sunday 10:55 a.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 1:15 p.m., for $418.
Sunday 2:15 p.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 4:35 p.m., for $436.
Sunday 5:35 p.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 7:55 p.m., for $401.
Monday 8:30 a.m. departure, arriving Tampa at 10:50 a.m., for $390 plus another night away.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Medium: A and B are both clean nonstops with a small fare difference, but they trade earlier arrival against Kara's preferred afternoon departure. C introduces a separate lower-fare, later-arrival alternative, requiring the learned preference to distinguish afternoon from merely late.
probes.gold_action: Recommend the 2:15 p.m. Sunday nonstop as the primary option, while retaining the morning and lower-fare late options as alternatives.
probes.label_rationale: Kara's return-time preference favors an afternoon departure, and her evidence also distinguishes that from simply taking the latest or cheapest return. The $18 premium over the morning flight is modest enough for the soft preference to decide, but not so small that the query itself establishes a universal best choice.
probes.query: Kara is returning to Tampa on Sunday after a pediatric mobility seminar that concludes Saturday evening. She has no Sunday program obligation and no fixed Monday-morning commitment. Three same-cabin nonstops are available, all within the trip budget. Which one should the planner recommend as the primary option?
